Where have our alirnmi gone5
? FROM
AN OWL
There was a time when Psi Upsilon had many
healthy, active alumni associations which met at
least once a
year, and some even more often, to
celebrate the Fraternity, brotherhood, and friend
ship. Unfortunately, only a small handful are still
active and alumni functions and Founders' Day
dinners and luncheons are
rapidly becoming extinct.
Many alumni associations exist now
solely to
own and manage a
fraternit)' house, and are in
danger of burnmg out the handful of loyal brothers
who spend most of their effort dealing with mainte
nance, msurance, furniture, and taxes. This, plus a
hostile admuiistration, provides little chance for
them to
experience the real rewards of brotherhood
and friendship.
Much of the blame for this decline lies with the
conunonly held behef that Psi Upsilon was
unique
and so elite that nothing ever had to change. What
was
ignored by everyone who could do something
about it was that society changed, that our alumni
were
moving and drifting away, and that the
demands of career and family made it aU too easy to
push a
complacent fraternity into the background or
completely out of one's life.
Your Fraternity has always claimed that once
you were initiated, you were a brother for hfe, and
Psi Upsilon has always implied that its alumni were
important and treasured resources.
Unfortunately,
too much emphasis of late, indeed, the sole focus,
seems to be on the "treasured" part, and many of
you no doubt feel that the only thing that Psi
Upsilon cares about is that check you might write,
whether to the Psi Upsilon Foundation for its
Annual Fund, or to your chapter for a
special
project.
Psi Upsilon desperately needs to have its alumni
involved at all levels, and has made support of
alumni groups a
top priority. The Executive Council
is doing its best to revive alumni functions. Re
cently, an alumni dinner, two receptions, and a
luncheon were held in San Diego, Long Beach,
Pasadena, and Beverly Hills. (For all of you
Easterners, all of those places are in southern
Cahfornia, home to almost 1,000 Psi U alumni.)
Over 40 brothers from chapters as diverse and far
apart as the Upsilon, Gamma, Phi, Mu, Epsilon,
Theta Theta, Delta Delta, Delta, Pi, Rho, Epsilon
Nu, Epsilon Omega, and Theta Epsilon had a
chance to meet each other and celebrate the
Fraternity.
One thing which stood out was that all of the
alumni who came cared about their Fraternity.
They also were
eager to know how Psi Upsilon was
faring and all were concerned about the "politically
correct" movement on
many campuses which
threatens all fraternities. What was most rewarding
to see was that everyone who attended, including
those who had drifted away from Psi Upsilon, was
proud to be a member of our
society, wanted to see
it continue and thrive, and looked forward to a
chance to meet with his brothers again.
The southern California functions occurred
solely because the Fraternity staff took the time and
much effort to make them successful. Future events
in California and elsewhere will need local interest
and local effort or
they won't happen. This is true
even of those events which currently take place
every year: including a fine dinner in Elmira, a
luncheon in Philadelphia, and annual dinners in
Detroit, Troy, San Francisco, and Seattie.
What your Fraternity often forgets, and what
undergraduates never seem to understand, is that
alumni need to be
courted. Recent
graduates and those of
25 or 50 years past
need to be given a
reason to stay involved.
Every member of the
Class of 1994 will face
a
myriad of distractions
and tasks, some of
which will be so time
consuming that Psi
Upsilon Fraternity will
become a faint memory
unless that member is
made to feel a
part of a
continuing institution.
Alumni associations
which meet frequently
and involve interaction among different generations
and chapters are vital to the health and welfare of �
Psi Upsilon and serve to keep the spirit alive after
graduation.
The gatherings in California are meant to be the
beginning of something very good for your Frater
nity. If you want to be involved and don't know of
an alumni association in your area, or if the one
you
belong to has been fading fast, then call the Interna
tional Office or write the President of the Executive
Council and let someone know of your interest. We
will be happy to help get something started. ?
"Alumni play a vital role
in the Fraternity. They
provide an
important link,
without which,
undergraduates of each
generation would know
little or
nothing of the rich
history of Psi Upsilon and of
the strength and durability
of brotherhood and
friendship."
Yours in the Bonds,
Charies M. Hall, Nu Alpha 71 (Washington & Lee)

Teach for America:
Psi U's involved with National Service
each for America is a national
teacher corps that recruits,
selects, trains, and supports
outstanding individuals who
commit two years to teach in
our nation's most underresourced urban and rural
public schools. Teach for
America is a
non-profit
organization, raising 100% of its $7 miUion
budget from private individuals, corporations, and
foundations. The mission of Teach for America is
to work dihgently toward the one
day when all
children will have equal access to an excellent
education. Two of the 15 Regional Directors of
Teach for America are Psi U alumni, Scott Moore,
Xi '91 (Wesleyan) and David Paulson, Chi '90
(Cornell).
Since its inception in 1989, Teach for America
has inspired 2,300 individuals to serve as teachers,
mentors, and role models for children in 15
geographic areas�
everj'where from South Central
Los Angeles to the South Bronx, from Washington,
D.C., to sites in rural and urban Louisiana and the
Mississippi Delta. Psi Upsilon alumni have been
with the program from the onset, first as
corps
members, and now as leaders. Both Brothers
Moore and Paulson completed their original twoyear commitments and now serve as
Regional
Directors in New Jersey and New Orleans, respec
tively. In that capacity, they are
responsible for
building the group of individuals into a united
corps who will remain advocates for educational
reform as they move into positions of authority
within the community. The vision is to create an
extensive network of leaders who will be linked by
a common belief that all children can learn and
that the future depends in large measure on the
abihty to tap uito our most precious resource:
children.
Teach for America is not simply a
placement
service, but a
professional corps that focuses on
professional growth, excellence in teaching,
education reform, and education advocacy.
Bringing teachers into classrooms is not enough.
As such. Teach for America corps members are
Brother Scott Moore, Xi '91 Wes/eyan (back row, far right) is flanked by the members of the 1993 New Jersey Corps.

workmg toward redefining what it means to be a
teacher. Across the country they are
involving
themselves with their students outside of school as
well as in the classroom. From city-wide children's
events to after- school sports programs to rural
advocacy coalitions, corps members are
going above
and beyond the call of duty.
What is inspiring about Teach for America, in
short, is how it leverages change. It impacts
hundreds of thousands of students by bringing them
teachers who believe in them. Yet as teachers
become involved in working with parents, neighbor
hoods, and towns, they have impacted the commu
nity. English language tutoring for parents,
computer literacy workshops, and African history
courses
open to the entire community are but a few
of the ways corps members reach out beyond the
classroom.
And finally, there are the corps members
themselves. Every year, 600 outstanding college
graduates enter the Teach for America program and
experience a
reality which changes the course of
their lives. Whether they discover a new career in
teaching, or
they move to the private sector,
government, or
public service, it is exciting to think
that Teach for America is providing a new
genera
tion of leaders who have met our
greatest social ills
head on in the classroom and now have the ability
to think critically about solutions.
Brothers Moore and Paulson are not the only Psi
U's involved in service programs, and not the only
Psi U's who have been drawn to Teach for America.
Brother Paulson taught both fourth and fifth grades
and coached an after-school flag football team in
New Orleans. Brother Eddie Gillmartin, Zeta '91
(Dartmouth) taught high school science for two
years. He says, "It was an incredible two-year
experience, and somehow, I think I learned the
most. There's no doubt that we all made strong
impressions on our kids. Unfortunately, I made my
greatest impression when I accidentally blew up an
Erlenmeyer flask filled with hydrogen gas."
Not all stories are as notorious as Brother
Gillmartin's, yet most
corps members have been
uniquely touched by interactions with the children.
Brother Charlie Schlegle, Phi '92 (Michigan), is
currently teaching fifth grade in New Orleans.
"TEA serves as an
intensely challenging opportu
nity to
really take concrete actions on social
problems, and it also serves as a
personal opportu
nity to be a
special influence in a
young person's
hfe. My goal is to be a
positive influence to the
children, similar to the positive influences of my
youth that helped me to be where I am."
In Houston, Psi U's are
having a remarkable
impact. Brother John Elliot, Kappa Phi '91

The Future is Ours
by Mark A. Williams, Phi '76 (Michigan)
Executive Director
There is much talk about the year 2000. We
hear it in advertising campaigns, we
point to it in
corporate annual reports, we see it in strategic
plans. The phrase usually goes something hke:
"We are
preparing for the year 2000 and beyond."
Six years from now in the year 2000, our
college campuses will be very different places from
what they are
today. Our campuses today are
very
different from what they were six years ago in
1988, 16 years ago in 1978, or 60 years ago in
1934.
There are some
things about the college
campuses of the year 2000 that we know today.
We know the demographics of the entering firstyear class. We know the approximate number of
students who will enter
college in the year 2000
and we know the racial, religious, and ethnic
heritage of those students. We know all that
because the Class of 2004 is alive today and
emolled in the sixth grade.
We know that technology, the emerging
"Information Superhighway," will dramatically
change the Hves of those entering college in the
year 2000. Most students enrolling in college
today get an electronic mail address along with
their student ID card (and if the E-mail address
isn't issued automatically, it's there for the
asking).
Alumni complain "my college is different" or
"Psi Upsilon is so different I don't recognize it" or
"its just not the Fraternity I remember." We who
are entrusted with the future of Psi Upsilon must
remember that today's campuses and students are
different from yesterday's and will be different
from tomorrow's. And that is probably good.
Succeeding generations seem to develop a
nostalgia for the era 20 years prior. After watch
ing a television show set in 1976 (the year I
'graduated from college), I shudder to think we are
about to suffer a revival of 1970's "culture." The
program reminded me that it was an era of bad
hair, bad clothes, and generally bad music.
Rut the program also reminded me that
today's entering freshmen need not spend much
time worrying whether their college careers will be
interrupted by military service in a time of war.
We know that budget restraints will continue
to limit resources available to our
college students
without regard to the multi-million or even
billion-dollar capital campaigns underway at most
of our alma maters. We know that student affairs
personnel and programming are
likely to be the
first to go.
We also know that fraternity will be just as
important, just as relevant, tomorrow as it is today
or as it was
yesterday (whenever your yesterday
was). In spite of, or rather, because
of that emerging technological world
we know is coming but don't fuUy
understand, the need for fraternity
will be as
great tomorrow as it was
yesterday.
Psi Upsilon succeeds because it
meets a basic human need to
associate, find and develop friend
ship, pursue common
goals, interact
with peers, share values, lead, follow,
learn, and socialize. The human
needs will remain the same in a world
that will be dramatically different.
It was never easy to be 18 years
old and it is not going to get any
easier in the next millenium. Young people will stiU
be maturing, testing limits, finding themselves, and
moving from dependence to independence. That's
what makes fraternity a
high risk venture but also
provides the opportunity for great success.
Where will the support come from? Who will
lead them? How will they react to values which
may differ from what they learned at home? In Psi
Upsilon we have the opportunity to change lives.
Compassion, fair play, honesty, tolerance, and
responsibility are lessons learned outside the
classroom.
If we don't get trapped by nostalgia for an era
long gone, the future is ours to mold and to
influence through the development of competent,
ethical leaders. ?
